bib.title: Asymptotic Lower Bounds for Stochastic Linear Bandits (Chapter 25, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: book chapter, Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press)

question: How does the action set (not just worst-case structure) determine the asymptotic regret of any consistent linear bandit policy, and can optimism achieve it?
contributions: Asymptotic lower bound on the design matrix for consistent policies on a finite action set (Thm 25.1)
Regret lower bound log(n)*c(A,theta) via an optimisation problem (Cor 25.2), matched by an upper bound (Thm 25.3, not proved)
A d=2,k=3 example showing optimistic algorithms (and Thompson sampling) can be arbitrarily worse than optimal

results.claim: Any consistent policy must make the confidence width of every suboptimal arm smaller than its gap: log(n)*||a||^2 in the inverse expected design matrix is at most Delta_a^2/2 in the limit.
results.setup: Finite action set A in R^d (|A|=k, spans R^d), rewards X_t=<A_t,theta>+standard Gaussian noise, unique optimal action, consistent policies (regret o(n^p) for all p>0)
results.quote: The theorem is saying that any consistent algorithm must prove statistically that all suboptimal arms are indeed suboptimal by making the size of the conﬁdence interval smaller than the suboptimality gap.

results.claim: Regret of any consistent policy grows at least c(A,theta)*log(n), where c(A,theta) is the minimum of sum_a alpha(a)Delta_a subject to ||a||^2_{H_alpha^-1} <= Delta_a^2/2 for all suboptimal a, H_alpha = sum alpha(a) a a^T.
results.setup: Finite action set A in R^d (|A|=k, spans R^d), rewards X_t=<A_t,theta>+standard Gaussian noise, unique optimal action, consistent policies (regret o(n^p) for all p>0)

results.claim: A matching upper bound exists: some policy attains limsup R_n/log(n) <= c(A,theta).
results.setup: Finite action set A in R^d (|A|=k, spans R^d), rewards X_t=<A_t,theta>+standard Gaussian noise, unique optimal action, consistent policies (regret o(n^p) for all p>0); not proved in the chapter

results.claim: In the 3-arm example (a1=e1, a2=e2, a3=(1-eps, gamma*eps), theta=(1,0), gamma>=1, small eps), the optimal asymptotic regret rate is 2*gamma^2 when 2*gamma^2 <= 2/eps: pull the clearly bad arm a2 about 2*gamma^2 times per log(n), never a3.
results.setup: d=2, k=3 arms, gaps Delta_a2=1, Delta_a3=eps
results.quote: Therefore, if ε is chosen suﬃciently small relative to γ, then the optimal rate of the regret is c(A, θ) = 2γ2

results.claim: In the same example, any consistent optimistic algorithm with confidence set Ct within a ball of radius c*sqrt(log n) in the V_t norm and gamma=Omega(c^2) suffers regret Omega(log(n)/eps), arbitrarily worse than 2*gamma^2*log(n) as eps -> 0.
results.setup: Same example; optimism At=argmax_a max_{theta~ in Ct}<a,theta~>; Ct contains theta w.h.p.
results.quote: which can be arbitrarily worse than the optimal rate!

results.claim: An optimistic algorithm plays the informative-but-bad arm a2 at most 1+4c^2 log(n) times, so it is forced to play near-optimal a3 at least Omega(log(n)/eps^2) times.
results.quote: which means that a2 will not be chosen more than 1 + 4c2 log(n) times.

results.claim: Key takeaway: optimism does not choose statistically suboptimal actions, but in linear bandits it can be optimal to play them more to learn about other actions; this extends to structured bandits where one action reveals others.
results.setup: Finite action set A in R^d (|A|=k, spans R^d), rewards X_t=<A_t,theta>+standard Gaussian noise, unique optimal action, consistent policies (regret o(n^p) for all p>0)
results.quote: The key take away from this is that optimistic algorithms do not choose actions that are statistically suboptimal, but for linear bandits it can be optimal to choose these actions more often to gain information about other actions.

results.claim: Thompson sampling is often empirically better than UCB but does not overcome this issue.
results.setup: Finite action set A in R^d (|A|=k, spans R^d), rewards X_t=<A_t,theta>+standard Gaussian noise, unique optimal action, consistent policies (regret o(n^p) for all p>0)
results.quote: While Thompson sampling is often empirically superior to UCB, it does not overcome the issues described here.

results.claim: Algorithms matching the lower bound solve the defining optimisation with an estimated theta; they are not practical in finite time and none is also near-minimax; a practical asymptotically optimal linear bandit algorithm is open.
results.setup: Finite action set A in R^d (|A|=k, spans R^d), rewards X_t=<A_t,theta>+standard Gaussian noise, unique optimal action, consistent policies (regret o(n^p) for all p>0)
results.quote: Unfortunately, these algorithms are not especially practical in ﬁnite time.

limits: Asymptotic only (n -> infinity) and for consistent policies; says nothing about finite-time regret
Finite action set, Gaussian noise, unique optimal action
Part 1 of Thm 25.1, Cor 25.2 and Thm 25.3 are not proved here (left as exercises or cited)
Optimism failure shown only for a constructed 3-arm example; the Omega(1/eps) claim is sketched, not fully proved
Matching algorithms are impractical in finite time (Notes)
practices: Do not assume UCB/optimism or Thompson sampling is asymptotically optimal for linear or structured bandits (Sec 25.2, Notes).
When actions share information, budget exploration of apparently bad but informative arms (Sec 25.2).

terms.definition: regret is sub-polynomial for any bandit in the class: Rn(A, θ) = o(np) for all p > 0 and θ
chooses At = argmax_a max over theta~ in Ct of <a, theta~>, with Ct a confidence set containing theta w.h.p.
